claims.text: Crystalline, near-equiatomic nanoparticles composed of five or more metals can form a single-phase solid solution.
Adding a refractory element such as tungsten to near-equiatomic multimetallic nanoparticles enhances their stability at 773–1173 K.
A tungsten-containing refractory multielement alloy is compatible with a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Adding tungsten to the nanoparticles causes formation or retention of a single-phase solid solution.
Adding a refractory element refines the nanoparticle grain structure.
The refractory-element addition suppresses grain growth during catalytic operation.
The refractory-element addition increases lattice distortion.
Suppressed grain growth and increased lattice distortion improve nanoparticle stability and durability.
Suppressed grain growth and increased lattice distortion improve catalytic performance.
Refractory-element-modified nanoparticles will exhibit better stability than nanoparticles without the refractory-element addition.
Refractory-element-modified nanoparticles will exhibit better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles.
Five-metal near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles are applicable to heterogeneous catalysis.
The proposed refractory-element intervention is applicable throughout the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
